samples.text:
Businesses play a big role in our society. Some people think a company only exist to make money for its owners, while others believe businesses should also help society. This essay will discuss both views, and I think businesses should do both.

People who believe profit is the main purpose have some good reasons. A business is not a charity, and the owners invest their money because they want to earn more. If a company does not make profit, it will close and all the workers will lose their job. Also, when companies are successful, they pay tax to the government, and the government can use this money for schools and hospitals. So making profit is already helping society in an indirect way.

However, other people argue that companies have a bigger responsibility. Big companies use a lot of natural resources and sometimes they pollute rivers and air. Some also pay very low salaries or sell unhealthy products to people. Because they have so much power, they should think about the effect on society, for example by protecting the environment, treating workers fairly and support local communities. Many customers today prefer to buy from companies who are responsible.

In my view, making profit is important, but it should not be the only goal. A company can be successful and also be good for society at the same time. For example, a factory can use clean energy and still earn money.

In conclusion, although profit is necessary for any business to survive, I believe businesses also has a responsibility to society. The best companies are the ones which can balance both of these things.
samples.why: Both views addressed and position stated early · relevant but general ideas · simple linking (Also, So, However) · adequate vocabulary with some repetition · several agreement and article errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The role of business in modern society is often debated. Some people argue that a company's primary purpose is to generate profits for its owners and shareholders, whereas others believe businesses have wider obligations to the communities in which they operate. In my opinion, profit is essential, but it should be pursued in a socially responsible way.

Those who emphasise profit argue that this is simply what businesses are designed to do. Investors risk their capital in the expectation of a return, and managers have a duty to use that money efficiently. Moreover, profitable companies already benefit society indirectly by creating jobs, paying taxes and developing products that people want. Some also suggest that social problems are better handled by governments and charities, which are directly accountable to the public.

On the other hand, many people believe that large companies have too much influence to ignore their wider impact. Business activities can damage the environment, exploit low-paid workers or harm consumers' health, and these costs are often paid by society rather than by the company itself. For this reason, it seems reasonable to expect businesses to reduce pollution, pay fair wages and behave ethically. Such behaviour can also be good for profits, since customers and employees increasingly prefer to be associated with responsible brands.

I believe these two goals are not necessarily in conflict. A company that treats its staff well tends to retain talented employees, and one that respect the environment avoids costly fines and reputational damage. Therefore, social responsibility should be seen as part of long-term business success rather than as an optional extra.

In conclusion, while making a profit is the fundamental aim of any business, I believe companies also have a clear responsibility to benefit society, and the most successful ones will be those that manage to achieve both.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant support · logical progression with clear central topics · good collocations (retain talented employees, reputational damage) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The question of what businesses are ultimately for has become more pressing as corporations grow in size and influence. One school of thought maintains that the sole purpose of a business is to maximise returns for its owners; another holds that companies bear a broader responsibility to society. While I accept that profitability is indispensable, I would argue that a narrow focus on shareholder returns is neither ethically defensible nor, in the long run, commercially wise.

Advocates of the profit-centred view make a coherent case. Owners and shareholders provide the capital that allows a company to exist, and they do so on the understanding that it will be managed in their financial interest. A profitable enterprise also contributes to society as a matter of course, by employing people, paying taxes and supplying goods and services that meet genuine demand. On this view, asking companies to pursue social goals risks diluting their efficiency and allowing unelected executives to make decisions that properly belong to governments.

However, this argument overlooks the extent to which business activity affects people who have no say in it. Pollution, unsafe working conditions and misleading marketing all impose costs on communities, workers and consumers, often while the company itself profits. Given the power that large firms wield, it is reasonable to expect them to take responsibility for these consequences. Moreover, responsible conduct increasingly aligns with self-interest: firms with strong ethical reputations tend to attract loyal customers and talented staff, and are better protected against regulatory and reputational risks.

In my view, then, profit and social responsibility should be seen as complementary rather than competing aims. A business must be financially sound to survive, but its legitimacy ultimately depends on the trust of the society in which it operates, and that trust must be earned.

In conclusion, although generating profit is a fundamental objective, businesses have a duty to consider their wider impact, and those that embrace this duty are likely to prove more successful and sustainable over time.
samples.why: Both views fully developed and evaluated · sophisticated, consistent position · skilful cohesion and paragraph management · wide, precise vocabulary (commercially wise, legitimacy) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
